blocks.p: The GPU Laboratory runs a small SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads) core in your browser. Its threads are grouped in warps; the threads of a warp share one instruction fetch and run it in lock-step, one thread per lane, each with its own 32 registers. An active mask says which lanes an instruction changes, and a reconvergence stack per warp lets the threads of a warp take different paths and meet again.

Every thread runs the RISC-V base instructions RV32I, less a few the core does not need. Five warp-control instructions are added on the custom-0 opcode: tmc sets the active mask, wspawn starts more warps, split and join bracket a branch on which the threads may disagree, and bar makes warps wait for one another. Their names and their R-type format follow the Vortex research GPU as its paper describes it.

Why it matters: a graphics processor gets its speed from many simple lanes rather than one clever pipeline, and its programs from code written for one thread. The core shows what that costs: lanes left idle when the threads of a warp branch apart, and the instructions that manage the mask. The Models view adds the ideas around it: thread indexing, latency hiding, coalescing and memory banks.
A second instruction set, the micro-ISA, is an introduction: seven instructions on four or eight lanes with a two-entry mask stack, chosen in the profile menu.

refs: Vortex: Extending the RISC-V ISA for GPGPU and 3D-Graphics Research
B. Tine, F. Elsabbagh, K. Yalamarthy, H. Kim. arXiv:2110.10857, 2021.

blocks.notice: The SIMT core and the micro-ISA are MAVILERA's teaching cores. They are not Vortex and not any product's GPU; MAVILERA makes no claim about the Vortex hardware or source code and is not affiliated with its authors. blocks.p: Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded: the laboratory runs entirely in your browser.

ol: Type a program in the editor, or open one from Templates: the laboratory programs, from a kernel without divergence to two warps meeting at a barrier, and two that fault on purpose.
Assemble it (Ctrl+Enter). Errors are listed in the console with their line.
Step (F10) or run (F5). Each step is one cycle, in which one warp issues one instruction. Step back (Shift+F10) undoes a step.
Watch the warps, their masks and stacks, and the threads' registers in the Threads tab of the memory pane; the counters give cycles, issued instructions, active lane-slots and the SIMT efficiency.
Choose a Core view to see the same run on the drawing of the core, or the Models view for the calculators.

blocks.p: The run ends when every warp has ended (tmc with a zero mask), or at a fault, which stops the core with a code and a message.

dl: One instruction per step: the editor, the listing with each word in hexadecimal and binary and its fields, the registers of the core and of each warp, the counters, the memory and the console.

The SIMT core with two warps of four lanes, drawn in this application's own layout. Each step is one cycle: the scheduler's choice of warp, the instruction broadcast to the lanes, the write gates driven by the active mask and the warp control are highlighted. warp_ctrl is shown by what it does, not by its logic. On a narrow screen the view shows one lane at a time: the mask strip of the coming issue, a button per lane, and what the chosen lane computes and writes; Whole drawing brings the drawing back.
The same core with one warp of eight lanes.
A tab of the Core views: the coming issue in detail, lane by lane: the mask bit, what the lane computes and whether it is written.

A tab of the Core views: one row per issue, a cell per lane with its mask bit (1 active, 0 idle and shaded). Masks-only count hides warp control, branches and each warp's launch and setup, so that the rows left are the work done under a mask.
A tab of the Core views: each issue with the active mask and the reconvergence stack after it.
A tab of the Core views: cycles, issued instructions, active lane-slots and SIMT efficiency of the program so far, and of the laboratory programs run here.
A tab of the Core views: done, fault, and each warp's mask and state over the cycles run so far.

Calculators for the ideas around the core: one loop on four machines, Amdahl's law, strip-mining, thread indexing, blocks on multiprocessors, latency hiding and occupancy, coalescing and shared-memory banks. They do not run the program in the editor.

The way into the CPU + GPU system: the core as a device of the RISC-V Laboratory's single-cycle processor, with its register map. Open the CPU + GPU system goes to that page. Kernel for a host gives the program in the editor as words to paste into a host program (Copy, or Download .s).

blocks.p: With the micro-ISA chosen, the views are Instructions, Masks · 4 lanes, Masks · 8 lanes, Models and CPU + GPU, and the Lanes tab of the memory pane shows each lane's registers.

Two profiles: two warps of four lanes, and one warp of eight lanes. Each warp has a program counter, an active mask, a state (ready, waiting at a barrier, or not running) and a reconvergence stack of four entries. Each cycle the scheduler takes the next ready warp in turn (round-robin) and issues one instruction to it; every instruction takes one cycle.

Memories: an instruction memory of 64 words and a data memory of 256 words, both from address 0. Every lane has its own port to the data memory, a simplification of the laboratory core; there is no cache and no memory latency.

dl: The active mask becomes rs1 of the lowest active thread. A zero mask ends the warp; tmc needs an empty stack.
In warp 0 only: starts warps 1 to rs1 − 1 at address rs2, every thread active, its registers 0.

Pushes a reconverge entry with the present mask. If bit 0 of rs1 divides the active threads, it also pushes an else entry with the other threads' mask and the address after split, and continues with the threads whose bit is 1.
Pops the stack: an else entry gives the other threads their turn from its address; a reconverge entry restores the mask.
The warp waits at barrier rs1 (0 or 1) until rs2 warps have reached it.
Reads an identity register of the thread: thread_index, lane_id, warp_id, block_index, block_size, kernel_args.

blocks.p: A conditional branch on which the active threads disagree is a fault: the core runs divergent code only between split and join, so a branch after split is uniform for each group. Other faults: an instruction outside the subset, a stack overflow, join on an empty stack, tmc with entries on the stack, a bad warp-control operand, and a load or store that is not word-aligned or lies outside the data memory.
Counters: cycles, issued warp-instructions and active lane-slots (the active lanes summed over the issues). SIMT efficiency = active lane-slots ÷ (issued × lanes).

This application's choices, where the laboratory core does not fix them: a faulting instruction is counted in the counters and takes one step; when every running warp waits at a barrier that no other warp will reach, the run stops before the cycle with a message; the register PC (next) is the PC of the warp that issues next.

dl: The additions of c[i] = a[i] + b[i] framed by what one instruction covers on a scalar pipeline, packed SIMD, a vector unit and a SIMT machine, with the instruction counts.
Speed-up S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / n) and efficiency S / n for a parallel fraction f on n lanes, with the ceiling 1 / (1 − f).
A loop strip-mined with a run-time vector length: AVL and vl of each strip, and the range of vl the rule permits.
A launch over n elements: blocks, threads, warps, the tail and the masks of the warps that are not full; where element i lies.
Whole blocks assigned to streaming multiprocessors, in waves, and the warps of one block.
A timeline of warps that each issue k instructions per load of latency L, the warps needed, (L − 1) / k + 1, and the occupancy a register file allows.
The memory blocks, transactions and bytes used of one warp's load at a stride.
The banks of a shared memory that a warp's access touches, and the cycles the busiest bank takes.

blocks.p: Where a model needs a rule that is not fixed by the idea itself, the rule is this application's and is stated in the tab's i button: the remainder of packed SIMD is done by scalar instructions; block b goes to SM b mod (number of SMs), a limited number at a time; the scheduler stays with a warp until it has issued its load, then takes the next ready warp in turn. None of them is the rule of a product.

sections.title: The core on a processor's bus

blocks.p: In the CPU + GPU system the SIMT core is a memory-mapped device of a RISC-V single-cycle processor at 0x5000_1000. A host program copies a kernel into the core's instruction memory and its data into the data memory, writes 1 to CTRL, polls STATUS while the core issues one warp-instruction per clock cycle, and reads the results back. Both machines step together, one clock cycle at a time.

dl: Bit 0 starts the kernel (warp 0 at address 0, every lane active); bit 1 clears DONE and FAULT.
Bit 0 BUSY, bit 1 DONE, bit 2 FAULT, bits 11:8 the fault code (8: a deadlock at a barrier).
CYCLES, ISSUED, ACTIVE: the counters of the kernel.
The instruction memory (64 words) and the data memory (256 words).

blocks.p: This register map is MAVILERA's own design, one way to attach such a core; it is not the only one.

ul: One instruction per line, with an optional label (loop:) and a comment after #.
.include "simt.inc" gives the names of the identity registers (THREAD_INDEX, LANE_ID, WARP_ID, BLOCK_INDEX, BLOCK_SIZE, KERNEL_ARGS); csrr reads them.
The code starts at address 0. .data starts the data memory at address 0; a label there can be an offset in a load or store: lw t1, x(t0).
Every thread runs the whole program. Use split before a branch on per-thread data and join where the paths meet; end each warp with tmc zero.
Not in the subset: auipc, jalr, byte and half-word loads and stores, fence, ecall and ebreak. The editor marks them, and the core faults on them.

blocks.p: File ▸ Exercise… lists practice exercises written for this application. Each opens with a starter program; its tests write data into memory, run your program until every warp has ended, and compare the memory it leaves with the expected values. No solutions are included.

blocks.p: The laboratory sends nothing anywhere. Your programs and settings are kept in this browser only.
